heading: Data Engineering & Analytics Projects
intro: Case studies emphasize the data problem, pipeline, architecture, operational trade-offs, and honest limitations—not just screenshots.

projects.title: Calgary Transit Live
projects.summary: A production GTFS and GTFS-Realtime pipeline with delayed vehicle playback, route context, stops, and alerts.
projects.problem: Vehicle positions are sparse and often omit the route and stop context needed for a useful map. The system joins realtime observations to static GTFS and exposes a stable frontend contract.
projects.architecture: Calgary feeds → Python poller → PostgreSQL transit schema → Express API → React/Leaflet, with NiceGUI serving the production bundle.
pipeline: Download and parse three protobuf feeds on a controlled schedule
Upsert current entities and retain a bounded vehicle observation history
Enrich trip, route, shape, stop, and alert context in PostgreSQL
Serve parameterized read queries through Express
Render playback approximately 75 seconds behind source time
outcomes: Deployed separate web, API, and worker services sharing PostgreSQL
Preserves source timestamps and distinguishes stopped and stale vehicles
Supports responsive route selection, upcoming stops, and alert context
limitations: Calgary LRT does not currently provide confirmed VehiclePositions in the observed feed
The public UI deliberately presents delayed playback rather than implying exact instantaneous location
Active-alert presentation still needs a production example when the feed supplies one

lab.heading: Project Lab: realtime data techniques
lab.intro: A closer look at the techniques and engineering concepts behind the public demonstration.

techniques.title: Sparse-feed enrichment
techniques.concept: Realtime records become useful when stable identifiers connect them to slower-changing reference data.
techniques.implementation: VehiclePositions supplies trip IDs and coordinates; PostgreSQL joins those trip IDs to static GTFS routes, shapes, stops, and service calendars before the API shapes a frontend response.
techniques.tradeoff: The join produces richer context without inventing data, but schedule-version drift can leave some realtime trips unmatched and must remain visible as a data-quality condition.

techniques.title: Delayed interpolation
techniques.concept: A small playback buffer can make discrete observations readable without pretending to predict the future.
techniques.implementation: The browser plays approximately 75 seconds behind the source and interpolates only between two observed positions, while stale and stopped thresholds preserve source honesty.
techniques.tradeoff: The map looks smoother and remains evidence-based, but it is intentionally delayed and cannot claim exact instantaneous vehicle location.

techniques.title: Independent feed transactions
techniques.concept: Related upstream feeds can have different failure modes, so one bad payload should not discard valid sibling updates.
techniques.implementation: Vehicle positions, trip updates, and alerts each own a transaction inside one polling cycle; failures roll back and log only the affected feed.
techniques.tradeoff: Useful partial freshness survives an upstream problem, while health reporting must disclose that the resulting snapshot may span different source times.

techniques.title: Freshness as a service contract
techniques.concept: An HTTP 200 and a database connection do not prove that a realtime product has current data.
techniques.implementation: The health endpoint reports source timestamps, recent vehicle counts, operating hours, and healthy, degraded, or expected after-hours states.
techniques.tradeoff: Monitoring and users receive an honest state, but thresholds and operating schedules become explicit operational configuration that must be maintained.

lab.working_method: Codex was used as an AI-assisted development tool. The portfolio owner reviewed and validated the resulting work.

projects.title: Data Platform Analytics Dashboard
projects.summary: A two-mode analytics product combining live PostgreSQL-backed Calgary pipeline quality with a committed theme-park analysis snapshot.
projects.problem: Show when an analytical question needs a fresh bounded query and when a validated versioned snapshot is the safer, faster delivery contract.
projects.architecture: Calgary GTFS pipeline → PostgreSQL aggregate queries → NiceGUI/ECharts, alongside validated snapshot JSON → quality contract → cached charts.
data_sources: Live aggregate transit tables in PostgreSQL
pipeline: Query bounded recent transit windows without exposing vehicle identifiers
Calculate route enrichment, ingestion cadence, and active-route coverage
Validate a small source-controlled snapshot before calculating attendance and revenue series
outcomes: Separates freshness-sensitive metrics from a low-change public snapshot
Publishes provenance timestamps, row counts, quality status, empty states, and accessible chart summaries
Adds private traffic charts without changing the anonymous path-and-time collection boundary
limitations: Theme-park values remain demonstration data and are not refreshed automatically
Transit coverage measures feed records and enrichment quality, not ridership or schedule performance
